claim: Transmission of the hedgehog signal across the plasma membrane by Smoothened is triggered by its interaction with cholesterol.
source: Previously we proposed that transmission of the hedgehog signal across the plasma membrane by Smoothened is triggered by its interaction with cholesterol (Luchetti et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Luchetti et al., 2016).

claim: Smoothened activation and hedgehog signaling are driven by a biochemically-defined, small fraction of membrane cholesterol, termed accessible cholesterol.
source: Using toxin-based sensors that distinguish between distinct pools of cholesterol, we find that Smoothened activation and hedgehog signaling are driven by a biochemically-defined, small fraction of membrane cholesterol, termed accessible cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using toxin-based sensors described in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing cholesterol accessibility by depletion of sphingomyelin amplifies hedgehog signaling.
source: Increasing cholesterol accessibility by depletion of sphingomyelin, which sequesters cholesterol in complexes, amplifies hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the effects of sphingomyelin depletion on hedgehog signaling.

claim: Sphingomyelin sequesters cholesterol in complexes.
source: Increasing cholesterol accessibility by depletion of sphingomyelin, which sequesters cholesterol in complexes, amplifies hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about sphingomyelin-cholesterol interactions.

claim: Hedgehog ligands increase cholesterol accessibility in the membrane of the primary cilium by inactivating Patched 1.
source: Hedgehog ligands increase cholesterol accessibility in the membrane of the primary cilium by inactivating the transporter-like protein Patched 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in cholesterol accessibility upon hedgehog ligand treatment.

claim: Trapping accessible cholesterol blocks hedgehog signal transmission across the membrane.
source: Trapping this accessible cholesterol blocks hedgehog signal transmission across the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using ALOD4 to trap accessible cholesterol.

claim: The organization of cholesterol in the ciliary membrane can be modified by extracellular ligands to control the activity of cilia-localized signaling proteins.
source: Our work shows that the organization of cholesterol in the ciliary membrane can be modified by extracellular ligands to control the activity of cilia-localized signaling proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing ligand-induced changes in ciliary cholesterol organization.

claim: Cholesterol directly binds and activates SMO.
source: We and others demonstrated that cholesterol directly binds and activates SMO and proposed that PTCH1 regulates SMO by restricting its access to cholesterol (Byrne et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Luchetti et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating cholesterol binding to SMO.

claim: PTCH1 regulates SMO by restricting its access to cholesterol.
source: We and others demonstrated that cholesterol directly binds and activates SMO and proposed that PTCH1 regulates SMO by restricting its access to cholesterol (Byrne et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Luchetti et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is presented as a proposed model.

claim: PTCH1 can bind and efflux sterols from cells.
source: Biochemical studies show that PTCH1 can bind and efflux sterols from cells (Bidet et al., 2011), and structural studies highlight the homology of PTCH1 to the cholesterol transporter Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) (Gong et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2019; Kowatsch et al., 2019; Qian et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2019a; Qi et al., 2018a; Qi et al., 2018b; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: PTCH1 has structural homology to the cholesterol transporter Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1).
source: Biochemical studies show that PTCH1 can bind and efflux sterols from cells (Bidet et al., 2011), and structural studies highlight the homology of PTCH1 to the cholesterol transporter Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) (Gong et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2019; Kowatsch et al., 2019; Qian et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2019a; Qi et al., 2018a; Qi et al., 2018b; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The resolution of PTCH1 cryo-EM structures is not high enough to distinguish cholesterol from other sterol lipids as PTCH1 substrates.
source: However, the resolution of the PTCH1 cryo-EM structures is not high enough to distinguish cholesterol from other sterol lipids as PTCH1 substrates, and PTCH1 transport activity has not yet been demonstrated in a purified system or at endogenous expression levels in cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the limitations of existing structural data.

claim: PTCH1 transport activity has not yet been demonstrated in a purified system or at endogenous expression levels in cells.
source: However, the resolution of the PTCH1 cryo-EM structures is not high enough to distinguish cholesterol from other sterol lipids as PTCH1 substrates, and PTCH1 transport activity has not yet been demonstrated in a purified system or at endogenous expression levels in cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of evidence in the literature.

claim: Cholesterol constitutes up to 50% of the lipid molecules in the plasma membrane.
source: A challenge to this model is presented by the fact that cholesterol constitutes up to 50% of the lipid molecules in the plasma membrane (Colbeau et al., 1971; Das et al., 2013; Lange et al., 1989; Touster et al., 1970): how can such an abundant lipid be kept away from SMO to prevent inappropriate pathway activation?
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work measuring cholesterol abundance.

claim: Oxysterols, phosphoinositides, endocannabinoids and arachidonic acid derivatives can bind and regulate SMO activity.
source: Indeed, other less abundant lipids can bind and regulate SMO activity, including oxysterols, phosphoinositides, endocannabinoids and arachidonic acid derivatives (Arensdorf et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2016; Khaliullina et al., 2015; Nachtergaele et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Side-chain oxysterols are synthesized through the enzymatic or non-enzymatic oxidation of cholesterol.
source: Side-chain oxysterols, synthesized through the enzymatic or non-enzymatic oxidation of cholesterol, are appealing alternatives to cholesterol because of their lower abundance, higher hydrophilicity and structural similarity to cholesterol (Corcoran and Scott, 2006; Dwyer et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and established knowledge.

claim: The CRISPR library targeted 1244 lipid-related genes compiled by the LIPID MAPS consortium.
source: Using our previously described strategy (Pusapati et al., 2018b) to identify positive and negative regulators of the HH pathway, we conducted focused loss-of-function CRISPR screens using a custom library targeting 1244 lipid-related genes compiled by the LIPID MAPS consortium (Supplementary file 1 provides a list of all genes and guide RNAs in the library).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: The CRISPR library targeted all annotated genes encoding enzymes involved in the synthesis or metabolism of lipids as well as proteins that bind or transport lipids.
source: This CRISPR library targeted all annotated genes encoding enzymes involved in the synthesis or metabolism of lipids as well as proteins that bind or transport lipids.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: The screens correctly identified Smo and Adrbk1 (or Grk2) as positive regulators.
source: The screens correctly identified all four positive controls included in the library: Smo and Adrbk1 (or Grk2) as positive regulators and Ptch1 and Sufu as negative regulators (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The screens correctly identified Ptch1 and Sufu as negative regulators.
source: The screens correctly identified all four positive controls included in the library: Smo and Adrbk1 (or Grk2) as positive regulators and Ptch1 and Sufu as negative regulators (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Gnas was identified as a gene that influences HH signaling.
source: In addition, genes previously known to influence HH signaling (Gnas) and protein trafficking at primary cilia (Inpp5e) were amongst the most significant hits (Chávez et al., 2015; Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2015; Regard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results and citations to prior work.

claim: Inpp5e was identified as a gene that influences protein trafficking at primary cilia.
source: In addition, genes previously known to influence HH signaling (Gnas) and protein trafficking at primary cilia (Inpp5e) were amongst the most significant hits (Chávez et al., 2015; Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2015; Regard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results and citations to prior work.

claim: Genes involved in phosphoinositide metabolism (Mtmr3 and Plcb3) were significant hits in the screen.
source: In addition to Inpp5e, other genes involved in phosphoinositide metabolism (Mtmr3 and Plcb3) were also significant hits.
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results.

claim: Pla2g3 was identified as a negative regulator of HH signaling.
source: Pla2g3, which encodes a secreted phospholipase, was identified as a negative regulator of HH signaling, an effect that may be related to its known role as a suppressor of ciliogenesis (Figure 1D) (Gijs et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pla2g3 has a known role as a suppressor of ciliogenesis.
source: Pla2g3, which encodes a secreted phospholipase, was identified as a negative regulator of HH signaling, an effect that may be related to its known role as a suppressor of ciliogenesis (Figure 1D) (Gijs et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Genes encoding enzymes in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway were positive regulators of HH signaling.
source: Statistically significant hits clustered in two major pathways: (1) genes encoding enzymes in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway were positive regulators of HH signaling and (2) genes encoding enzymes in the sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway were negative regulators (positive regulators are shown in blue and negative regulators in orange in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Genes encoding enzymes in the sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway were negative regulators of HH signaling.
source: Statistically significant hits clustered in two major pathways: (1) genes encoding enzymes in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway were positive regulators of HH signaling and (2) genes encoding enzymes in the sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway were negative regulators (positive regulators are shown in blue and negative regulators in orange in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mutations in Dhcr7 and Sc5d impair HH signaling in target cells.
source: Mutations in Dhcr7 and Sc5d, which encode enzymes that catalyze the terminal steps in cholesterol biosynthesis, impair HH signaling in target cells and cause the congenital malformation syndromes Smith-Lemli-Opitz and lathosterolosis, respectively (Blassberg et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 2003; Horvat et al., 2011; Porter and Herman, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in Dhcr7 and Sc5d cause the congenital malformation syndromes Smith-Lemli-Opitz and lathosterolosis, respectively.
source: Mutations in Dhcr7 and Sc5d, which encode enzymes that catalyze the terminal steps in cholesterol biosynthesis, impair HH signaling in target cells and cause the congenital malformation syndromes Smith-Lemli-Opitz and lathosterolosis, respectively (Blassberg et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 2003; Horvat et al., 2011; Porter and Herman, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Many genes encoding enzymes in the pathway that converts squalene to cholesterol were statistically significant hits in the HiSHH-Bot10% screen.
source: In addition to these genes, many of the genes encoding enzymes in the pathway that converts squalene to cholesterol were statistically significant hits with a FDR-corrected p-value threshold of 0.1 in the HiSHH-Bot10% screen (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CRISPR-mediated loss-of-function mutations in Lss impaired the transcriptional induction of endogenous Gli1.
source: CRISPR-mediated loss-of-function mutations in Lss, required for an early step in the pathway, and in Dhcr7 and Dhcr24, required for the terminal steps, impaired the transcriptional induction of endogenous Gli1 (an immediate target gene used as a measure of signaling strength) (Figure 2B and C; CRISPR-edited alleles shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: CRISPR-mediated loss-of-function mutations in Dhcr7 impaired the transcriptional induction of endogenous Gli1.
source: CRISPR-mediated loss-of-function mutations in Lss, required for an early step in the pathway, and in Dhcr7 and Dhcr24, required for the terminal steps, impaired the transcriptional induction of endogenous Gli1 (an immediate target gene used as a measure of signaling strength) (Figure 2B and C; CRISPR-edited alleles shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: CRISPR-mediated loss-of-function mutations in Dhcr24 impaired the transcriptional induction of endogenous Gli1.
source: CRISPR-mediated loss-of-function mutations in Lss, required for an early step in the pathway, and in Dhcr7 and Dhcr24, required for the terminal steps, impaired the transcriptional induction of endogenous Gli1 (an immediate target gene used as a measure of signaling strength) (Figure 2B and C; CRISPR-edited alleles shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The abundance of cholesterol was reduced in Dhcr7-/- and Dhcr24-/- cells.
source: Quantitative mass spectrometry measurements and intact cell staining with a cholesterol-binding probe confirmed that the abundance of cholesterol was reduced in Dhcr7-/- and Dhcr24-/- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and probe staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The abundances of 7-dehydrocholesterol and desmosterol were elevated in Dhcr7-/- and Dhcr24-/- cells, respectively.
source: Conversely, the abundances of substrates for Dhcr7 and Dhcr24, 7-dehydrocholesterol and desmosterol, respectively, were elevated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: HH signaling in Lss-/- cells could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol.
source: HH signaling in both Lss-/- and Dhcr7-/- cells, but not in Dhcr24-/- cells, could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol, pointing to cholesterol deficiency as the cause of impaired HH signaling (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: HH signaling in Dhcr7-/- cells could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol.
source: HH signaling in both Lss-/- and Dhcr7-/- cells, but not in Dhcr24-/- cells, could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol, pointing to cholesterol deficiency as the cause of impaired HH signaling (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: HH signaling in Dhcr24-/- cells could not be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol.
source: HH signaling in both Lss-/- and Dhcr7-/- cells, but not in Dhcr24-/- cells, could be rescued with the addition of exogenous cholesterol, pointing to cholesterol deficiency as the cause of impaired HH signaling (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Rescue of HH signaling defects in Dhcr7-/- cells by exogenous cholesterol has been demonstrated previously.
source: Rescue of HH signaling defects in Dhcr7-/- cells by exogenous cholesterol has also been demonstrated previously (Blassberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DHCR24 is the only enzyme that is required for cholesterol biosynthesis but dispensable for 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol synthesis.
source: 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol is a unique oxysterol that is not synthesized from cholesterol but rather made through a shunt pathway that closely parallels the post-squalene cholesterol biosynthesis pathway (Figure 2A). Exogenously added 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol can bind and activate SMO, so it has been proposed that this oxysterol (present at ~1% of the levels of cholesterol in cells) may be an endogenous SMO agonist regulated by PTCH1 (Qi et al., 2019b; Raleigh et al., 2018). Interestingly, DHCR24 is only used in the Kandutsch-Russell and Bloch pathways for cholesterol synthesis but not in the shunt pathway for the synthesis of 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol (Sharpe and Brown, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and the pathway diagram in Figure 2A.

claim: Loss of DHCR24 blocks HH signaling without reducing 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol abundance.
source: The fact that loss of DHCR24 blocks HH signaling (Figure 2A and C) without reducing 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) suggests that cholesterol rather than 24(S), 25-epoxycholesterol regulates HH signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cholesterol itself, rather than a precursor or a metabolite, is the endogenous sterol lipid that regulates SMO activation.
source: In summary, the data from our genetic screen support the view that cholesterol itself, rather than a precursor or a metabolite, is the endogenous sterol lipid that regulates SMO activation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the genetic screen results.

claim: Sptlc2 is the first committed step in sphingolipid synthesis from L-serine and palmitoyl-CoA.
source: Top hits from this screen include Sptlc2, the first committed step in sphingolipid synthesis from L-serine and palmitoyl-CoA, as well as Sgms1, which converts ceramide to sphingomyelin (SM).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of sphingolipid biosynthesis.

claim: Sgms1 converts ceramide to sphingomyelin (SM).
source: Top hits from this screen include Sptlc2, the first committed step in sphingolipid synthesis from L-serine and palmitoyl-CoA, as well as Sgms1, which converts ceramide to sphingomyelin (SM).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of sphingolipid biosynthesis.

claim: The identification of Sgms1 suggests that SM is the relevant product of the sphingolipid pathway that attenuates HH signaling.
source: The identification of Sgms1 suggests that SM is the relevant product of the sphingolipid pathway that attenuates HH signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the screen results.

claim: Myriocin is a fungal antibiotic that inhibits SPTLC2.
source: Myriocin is a fungal antibiotic that inhibits SPTLC2 (Figure 3A) and is commonly used to deplete SM in cells (Courtney et al., 2018; Tafesse et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and established knowledge.

claim: Myriocin is commonly used to deplete SM in cells.
source: Myriocin is a fungal antibiotic that inhibits SPTLC2 (Figure 3A) and is commonly used to deplete SM in cells (Courtney et al., 2018; Tafesse et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Myriocin treatment potentiated the response to SHH in NIH/3T3 cells.
source: Myriocin treatment potentiated the response to SHH in NIH/3T3 cells, as measured by the transcriptional induction of Gli1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Myriocin was sufficient to activate HH signaling in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) even in the absence of added HH ligands.
source: In mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), myriocin was sufficient to activate HH signaling even in the absence of added HH ligands (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Myriocin potentiated the effect of SHH on mouse spinal neural progenitor cells (NPCs), substantially reducing the concentration of SHH required to drive motor neuron differentiation.
source: Mouse spinal neural progenitor cells (NPCs) differentiate into Olig2-expressing motor neuron progenitors in response to moderate concentrations of SHH. Myriocin potentiated the effect of SHH on NPCs, substantially reducing the concentration of SHH required to drive motor neuron differentiation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fumonisin B1 amplified HH signaling.
source: First, fumonisin B1, a mycotoxin structurally distinct from myriocin that inhibits a different step in SM synthesis (Figure 3A), also amplified HH signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The potentiating effect of myriocin on HH signaling could be reversed by the exogenous administration of SM.
source: Second, the potentiating effect of myriocin on HH signaling could be reversed by the exogenous administration of SM (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Increasing SM levels in cells using a low-dose of staurosporine reduced HH signaling strength.
source: Finally, increasing SM levels in cells using a low-dose of staurosporine had the expected opposite effect: reduction of HH signaling strength (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) (Maekawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: SM is localized in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: SM is localized in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane (Bretscher, 1972; Murate and Kobayashi, 2016; Verkleij et al., 1973) where it plays key roles in its lateral organization, including the formation of ordered membrane microdomains that can influence protein trafficking, signaling and other processes (Levental and Veatch, 2016; Simons and Ikonen, 2000; Simons and Ikonen, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SM plays key roles in the lateral organization of the plasma membrane, including the formation of ordered membrane microdomains.
source: SM is localized in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane (Bretscher, 1972; Murate and Kobayashi, 2016; Verkleij et al., 1973) where it plays key roles in its lateral organization, including the formation of ordered membrane microdomains that can influence protein trafficking, signaling and other processes (Levental and Veatch, 2016; Simons and Ikonen, 2000; Simons and Ikonen, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Myriocin did not significantly alter the abundances of the HH pathway proteins GLI3, SMO, SUFU or PTCH1.
source: Myriocin did not significantly alter the abundances of the HH pathway proteins GLI3, SMO, SUFU or PTCH1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and also did not change either the frequency or the length of primary cilia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Myriocin did not change either the frequency or the length of primary cilia.
source: Myriocin did not significantly alter the abundances of the HH pathway proteins GLI3, SMO, SUFU or PTCH1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and also did not change either the frequency or the length of primary cilia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PTCH1 and GPR161 were properly localized in the ciliary membrane in myriocin-treated cells and were cleared from cilia in response to SHH addition.
source: However, both proteins were properly localized in the ciliary membrane in myriocin-treated cells and were cleared (as expected) from cilia in response to SHH addition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Myriocin potentiated SMO ciliary accumulation in NIH/3T3 cells.
source: The SHH-triggered accumulation of SMO in primary cilia is required for initiation of HH signaling in the cytoplasm (Corbit et al., 2005). Myriocin potentiated SMO ciliary accumulation in NIH/3T3 cells, suggesting that SM depletion enhances SMO activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HH signaling in cells treated with myriocin was blocked by the SMO antagonist Vismodegib.
source: HH signaling in cells treated with myriocin was blocked by the SMO antagonist Vismodegib (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Myriocin failed to activate HH signaling in Smo-/- cells.
source: Myriocin also failed to activate HH signaling in Smo-/- cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Myriocin acts on SMO, or at a step upstream of SMO.
source: Both observations suggest that myriocin acts on SMO, or at a step upstream of SMO.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with Vismodegib and Smo-/- cells.

claim: SMO has two potential cholesterol-binding sites: one in the CRD and a second in the TMD.
source: SMO has multiple ligand binding sites: one in the extracellular cysteine-rich domain (CRD) that binds cholesterol and oxysterols and another in the transmembrane domain (TMD) that binds to diverse SMO ligands and to sterols (Byrne et al., 2018; Deshpande et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2019b; Sharpe et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the CRD site abolish sterol binding and responses to SHH.
source: Mutations in the CRD site abolish sterol binding and responses to SHH; mutations in the more superficial region of the TMD site prevent SMO activation by synthetic agonists like Smoothened Agonist (SAG) but do not affect responses to SHH (Figure 4B) (Byrne et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Luchetti et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the TMD site prevent SMO activation by synthetic agonists like SAG but do not affect responses to SHH.
source: Mutations in the CRD site abolish sterol binding and responses to SHH; mutations in the more superficial region of the TMD site prevent SMO activation by synthetic agonists like Smoothened Agonist (SAG) but do not affect responses to SHH (Figure 4B) (Byrne et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Luchetti et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the sterol-binding CRD site (D99A/Y134F) reduced myriocin-driven activation of HH signaling.
source: Previously defined mutations in the sterol-binding CRD site (D99A/Y134F, Figure 4B), which abrogate cholesterol binding by disrupting a key hydrogen bond with the 3β-hydroxyl of cholesterol, reduced myriocin-driven activation (Figure 4C) (Byrne et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A mutation (D477G) in the TMD site failed to diminish myriocin-induced signaling.
source: In contrast, a mutation (D477G, Figure 4B) in the TMD site failed to diminish myriocin-induced signaling (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SM regulates SMO activity by controlling the availability of cellular cholesterol that can bind to SMO.
source: The observation that mutations in the CRD of SMO, a well-defined binding site for cholesterol (Byrne et al., 2016), attenuated the effects of SM depletion (Figure 4C) suggested that SM regulates SMO activity by controlling the availability of cellular cholesterol that can bind to SMO.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with SMO mutants.

claim: Plasma membrane cholesterol is organized in three pools: a fixed pool essential for membrane integrity, a SM-sequestered pool with low chemical activity and a third ('accessible') pool with higher chemical activity.
source: These studies have led to the proposal that plasma membrane cholesterol is organized in three pools: a fixed pool essential for membrane integrity, a SM-sequestered pool with low chemical activity and a third ('accessible') pool with higher chemical activity that is available to interact with proteins and transport to the ER (Das et al., 2014; Lange et al., 2004; Radhakrishnan et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The distribution of cholesterol between the sequestered and accessible pools is determined by the ratio of cholesterol to SM.
source: The distribution of cholesterol between the sequestered and accessible pools is determined by the ratio of cholesterol to SM: SM depletion (or cholesterol addition) leads to an increase in accessible cholesterol (Figure 5A) (Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PFO* binds to the accessible pool of cholesterol.
source: Instead, protein probes derived from lipid-binding toxins have been recently developed to distinguish between the accessible and sequestered pools in intact membranes or cells (Figure 5A): PFO*, derived from the bacterial toxin Perfringolysin O, binds to the accessible pool of cholesterol and OlyA, derived from the fungal toxin Osterolysin A, binds to SM-cholesterol complexes (Das et al., 2013; Endapally et al., 2019a; Flanagan et al., 2009; Skočaj et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: OlyA binds to SM-cholesterol complexes.
source: Instead, protein probes derived from lipid-binding toxins have been recently developed to distinguish between the accessible and sequestered pools in intact membranes or cells (Figure 5A): PFO*, derived from the bacterial toxin Perfringolysin O, binds to the accessible pool of cholesterol and OlyA, derived from the fungal toxin Osterolysin A, binds to SM-cholesterol complexes (Das et al., 2013; Endapally et al., 2019a; Flanagan et al., 2009; Skočaj et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: OlyA_E69A binds to both free SM and SM-cholesterol complexes.
source: A useful point mutant of OlyA (OlyA_E69A) binds to both free SM and SM-cholesterol complexes, allowing measurement of total SM (Figure 5A) (Endapally et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Treatment of cells with myriocin decreased both OlyA and OlyA_E69A staining.
source: Treatment of cells with myriocin decreased both OlyA and OlyA_E69A staining, consistent with SM depletion (Figure 5B and C); staining was restored by the addition of exogenous egg SM (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Myriocin treatment and cholesterol loading increased PFO* staining.
source: Myriocin treatment and cholesterol loading increased PFO* staining, showing that both treatments increased the level of accessible cholesterol in the plasma membrane (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The depletion of SM with myriocin or other pharmacological agents does not change the abundances of total cellular cholesterol or plasma membrane cholesterol.
source: The depletion of SM with myriocin or other pharmacological agents does not change the abundances of total cellular cholesterol or plasma membrane cholesterol (Das et al., 2014; Tafesse et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reducing accessible cholesterol in myriocin-treated cells with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) decreased SHH-induced activation of the GLI-GFP reporter.
source: Reducing accessible cholesterol in myriocin-treated cells with methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD), measured by PFO* staining, decreased SHH-induced activation of the GLI-GFP reporter (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SM impairs HH signaling by sequestering cholesterol into complexes where it is inaccessible to SMO.
source: These results, together with the requirement of the cholesterol-binding CRD for the potentiating effect of myriocin (Figure 4C), support the model that SM impairs HH signaling by sequestering cholesterol into complexes where it is inaccessible to SMO.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Purified SMO is constitutively active in nano-discs containing physiological levels of cholesterol in the absence of SM.
source: This conclusion is also consistent with the observation that purified SMO is constitutively active in nano-discs containing physiological levels of cholesterol in the absence of SM (Myers et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ALOD4 selectively traps accessible cholesterol on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane without altering cholesterol levels in the cell or plasma membrane.
source: Unlike a reagent like MβCD, which extracts cholesterol from cells, ALOD4 selectively traps accessible cholesterol on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane without altering cholesterol levels in the cell or plasma membrane (Figure 6A) (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both ALOD4 and MβCD blocked HH signaling when added to cells.
source: Despite very different mechanisms of action, both ALOD4 and MβCD blocked HH signaling when added to cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ALOD4 induced the expression of Hmgcr.
source: In a control experiment, ALOD4 induced the expression of Hmgcr, the gene encoding the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase, which is known to be induced when accessible cholesterol is depleted (Figure 6C) (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ALOD4 did not change the frequency of ciliation.
source: ALOD4 did not change the frequency of ciliation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: HH signaling is enhanced by myriocin, which increases accessible cholesterol.
source: In summary, HH signaling is enhanced by myriocin, which increases accessible cholesterol (Figure 5E), but inhibited by ALOD4, which decreases accessible cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: HH signaling is inhibited by ALOD4, which decreases accessible cholesterol.
source: In summary, HH signaling is enhanced by myriocin, which increases accessible cholesterol (Figure 5E), but inhibited by ALOD4, which decreases accessible cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with ALOD4.

claim: Neither myriocin nor ALOD4 change total cholesterol abundance in cells.
source: Neither myriocin nor ALOD4 change total cholesterol abundance in cells (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017; Tafesse et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Accessible cholesterol is the thermodynamically distinct fraction of total cholesterol that is relevant for the regulation of SMO in HH signaling.
source: We conclude that accessible cholesterol is the thermodynamically distinct fraction of total cholesterol that is relevant for the regulation of SMO in HH signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with myriocin and ALOD4.

claim: The regulation of SMO by PTCH1 occurs at primary cilia.
source: The regulation of SMO by PTCH1 occurs at primary cilia, the only post-Golgi compartment in the cell where both proteins can be found localized together (Rohatgi et al., 2009; Rohatgi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ciliary membrane is thought to have a different lipid and protein composition than the plasma membrane.
source: Since the ciliary membrane is thought to have a different lipid and protein composition than the plasma membrane (Nachury and Mick, 2019), we compared PFO*, OlyA and OlyA_E69A staining in the ciliary membrane relative to the plasma membrane using confocal microscopy.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ratio of SM to cholesterol is high in the ciliary membrane.
source: In untreated cells, the C/P ratio was significantly higher for OlyA_E69A staining compared to OlyA or PFO* staining (Figure 7A). This suggests that the ratio of SM to cholesterol, which determines the abundance of accessible cholesterol, is high in the ciliary membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the probe staining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Most cilia of untreated cells did not show distinctive staining for SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA) or accessible cholesterol (PFO*).
source: Indeed, while OlyA_E69A staining of total SM was readily detectable in cilia, most cilia of untreated cells did not show distinctive staining for SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA) or accessible cholesterol (PFO*) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cholesterol loading increased the C/P ratio of SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA staining).
source: Cholesterol loading increased the C/P ratio of SM-cholesterol complexes (OlyA staining, Figure 7B and D), showing that a significant proportion of SM molecules at cilia are free to pair with exogenously added cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: Myriocin treatment increased the amount of accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane relative to the plasma membrane.
source: Myriocin treatment, which reduced SM levels in both the plasma membrane and the ciliary membrane (Figure 5B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), increased the amount of accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane relative to the plasma membrane (PFO* staining, Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: SM provides the major restraint on cholesterol accessibility at cilia.
source: Indeed, myriocin had a greater effect on the C/P ratio of accessible cholesterol compared to even cholesterol loading, suggesting that SM provides the major restraint on cholesterol accessibility at cilia (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The ciliary membrane is significantly more resistant (compared to the plasma membrane) to permeabilization by both PFO and cholesterol-binding detergents like digitonin.
source: A high ratio of SM to cholesterol provides a potential explanation for the observation that the ciliary membrane is significantly more resistant (compared to the plasma membrane) to permeabilization by both PFO and cholesterol-binding detergents like digitonin (Breslow et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SHH did not induce much of a change in PFO* staining of the bulk plasma membrane.
source: SHH did not induce much of a change in PFO* staining of the bulk plasma membrane, measured by flow cytometry (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: SHH led to a rapid increase in accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane when cells were treated with myriocin or loaded with cholesterol.
source: In contrast, SHH led to a rapid increase in accessible cholesterol in the ciliary membrane, either when cells were treated with myriocin or when cells were loaded with cholesterol (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: SHH did not change ciliary PFO* staining in Ptch1-/- cells.
source: SHH did not change ciliary PFO* staining in Ptch1-/- cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Activation of signaling with SAG did not cause significant changes in accessible cholesterol at the ciliary membrane.
source: In addition, activation of signaling with SAG, which bypasses PTCH1 and directly activates SMO, also did not cause significant changes in accessible cholesterol at the ciliary membrane (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The SHH-induced change in accessible cholesterol at primary cilia is dependent on PTCH1 activity.
source: Both controls show that the SHH-induced change in accessible cholesterol at primary cilia is dependent on PTCH1 activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results with Ptch1-/- cells and SAG treatment.

claim: Only a fraction of total plasma membrane cholesterol is relevant to the regulation of HH signaling.
source: First, only a fraction of total plasma membrane cholesterol is relevant to the regulation of HH signaling. This thermodynamically distinct pool of accessible cholesterol with high chemical activity ranges from ~2% of total plasma membrane cholesterol in lipid depleted cells to ~15% of total plasma membrane cholesterol in lipid replete cells (Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The changes in accessible cholesterol that regulate SMO are confined to a subcellular compartment, the primary cilium.
source: Second, the changes in accessible cholesterol that regulate SMO are confined to a subcellular compartment, the primary cilium, where PTCH1, SMO and the cytoplasmic signaling machinery downstream of SMO are localized.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing compartmentalized changes in accessible cholesterol.

claim: The lipid composition of primary cilia may be dynamically altered to control the activity or trafficking of cilia-localized proteins.
source: Phosphoinositides and oxysterols are examples of other lipids whose abundances in the ciliary membrane are different from the plasma membrane (Chávez et al., 2015; Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2015; Raleigh et al., 2018), supporting the general principle that the lipid composition of primary cilia may be dynamically altered to control the activity or trafficking of cilia-localized proteins (Nachury and Mick, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and inference from the current findings.

claim: SCAP senses accessible cholesterol in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to regulate the transcription of genes that control cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: Another pathway that detects and responds to accessible cholesterol is the SCAP/SREBP signaling system, which provided an important precedent (and inspiration) for our work (Brown et al., 2018; Brown and Goldstein, 2009). SCAP senses accessible cholesterol in a specific subcellular compartment, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), to regulate the transcription of genes that control cholesterol biosynthesis (Radhakrishnan et al., 2008; Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Continual transport of cholesterol from the plasma membrane to the ER ensures that information about changes in plasma membrane cholesterol accessibility is transmitted to the ER, where SCAP is localized.
source: Continual transport of cholesterol from the plasma membrane to the ER ensures that information about changes in plasma membrane cholesterol accessibility is transmitted to the ER, where SCAP is localized (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PTCH1 may selectively transport the pool of accessible cholesterol to a yet unknown membrane or protein acceptor.
source: We suggest that PTCH1 may selectively transport the pool of accessible cholesterol (rather than the fixed or SM-bound pool) to a yet unknown membrane or protein acceptor (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Selective transport of accessible cholesterol has been previously proposed for other cholesterol transporter proteins.
source: Selective transport of accessible cholesterol has been previously proposed for other cholesterol transporter proteins (Lange and Steck, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PTCH1 could transport cholesterol from the ciliary membrane to a sterol transport protein or a membrane compartment in the cytoplasm.
source: The direction of sterol transfer by PTCH1 remains uncertain: it could transport cholesterol in the same direction as its relative NPC1 (from the ciliary membrane to a sterol transport protein or a membrane compartment in the cytoplasm) or in an outward direction from the ciliary membrane to an extracellular acceptor (see arrows labeled 1 and 2 in Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is speculative and presents alternative hypotheses.

claim: PTCH1 could transport cholesterol in an outward direction from the ciliary membrane to an extracellular acceptor.
source: The direction of sterol transfer by PTCH1 remains uncertain: it could transport cholesterol in the same direction as its relative NPC1 (from the ciliary membrane to a sterol transport protein or a membrane compartment in the cytoplasm) or in an outward direction from the ciliary membrane to an extracellular acceptor (see arrows labeled 1 and 2 in Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is speculative and presents alternative hypotheses.

claim: The prominent localization of PTCH1 at and around the base of primary cilia raises the possibility that PTCH1 functions at the ciliary pocket to deplete accessible cholesterol from the ciliary membrane.
source: The prominent localization of PTCH1 at and around the base of primary cilia (Rohatgi et al., 2007) raises the possibility that PTCH1 functions at the ciliary pocket to deplete accessible cholesterol from the ciliary membrane (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from localization data.

claim: The cholesterol pumping activity of PTCH1 will be opposed by the continual leak of cholesterol back into the cilium from the large pool in the plasma membrane or by the delivery of cholesterol from sterol binding proteins in the cytoplasm.
source: The cholesterol pumping activity of PTCH1 will be opposed by the continual leak of cholesterol back into the cilium from the large pool in the plasma membrane (since the ciliary membrane is continuous with the plasma membrane) or by the delivery of cholesterol from sterol binding proteins in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference about membrane dynamics.

claim: The 'pump-leak' model may be energetically sustainable because PTCH1 is tasked with reducing accessible cholesterol only over the small surface area of the ciliary membrane.
source: This 'pump-leak' model may be energetically sustainable because PTCH1 is tasked with reducing accessible cholesterol only over the small surface area of the ciliary membrane (~400 fold smaller than that of the plasma membrane) (Nachury, 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference about energetics.

claim: When PTCH1 is inactivated by HH ligands, accessible cholesterol levels in primary cilia will rapidly rise due to unopposed lateral movement from the plasma membrane or delivery from cytosolic sterol transfer proteins, resulting in SMO activation.
source: When PTCH1 is inactivated by HH ligands, accessible cholesterol levels in primary cilia will rapidly rise due to unopposed lateral movement from the plasma membrane or delivery from cytosolic sterol transfer proteins, resulting in SMO activation.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the proposed model.

claim: The level of SM in the ciliary membrane determines the set-point for how much cholesterol needs to be transported by PTCH1 to reduce accessible cholesterol below the threshold required to activate SMO.
source: In this model, the level of SM in the ciliary membrane determines the set-point for how much cholesterol needs to be transported by PTCH1 to reduce accessible cholesterol below the threshold required to activate SMO.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the proposed model.

claim: Depleting SM raises the demands on PTCH1 transport activity and hence makes cells hyper-sensitive to PTCH1-inactivating HH ligands.
source: Depleting SM (or loading cells with cholesterol) raises the demands on PTCH1 transport activity and hence makes cells hyper-sensitive to PTCH1-inactivating HH ligands.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: In some cell types (MEFs), PTCH1 cannot completely overcome the effect of SM depletion, leading to SMO activation even in the absence of any SHH.
source: In some cell types (MEFs, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), PTCH1 cannot completely overcome the effect of SM depletion, leading to SMO activation even in the absence of any SHH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Other phospholipids can also complex cholesterol and may reduce its chemical activity at the ciliary membrane.
source: Our focus on SM was driven by the results of our screen, but we note that other phospholipids can also complex cholesterol and may reduce its chemical activity at the ciliary membrane (Keller et al., 2000; Lange et al., 2013; McConnell and Radhakrishnan, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SMO has two potential cholesterol-binding sites: one in the CRD and a second deep in the TMD.
source: SMO has two potential cholesterol-binding sites: one in the CRD (tested in Figure 4C) and a second deep in the TMD (Byrne et al., 2016; Deshpande et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Luchetti et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in either the CRD or TMD cholesterol-binding sites prevent the activation of signaling by HH ligands.
source: Mutations in either site prevent the activation of signaling by HH ligands, implicating both in the regulation of SMO by PTCH1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The TMD site has been proposed to obtain cholesterol from the inner leaflet through an opening between two transmembrane helices.
source: The extracellular CRD site is ~12 angstroms away from the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane (Luchetti et al., 2016), while the TMD site has been proposed to obtain cholesterol from the inner leaflet through an opening between two transmembrane helices (Deshpande et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PTCH1 has been proposed to inhibit SMO by reducing cholesterol abundance in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: In the latter case, PTCH1 has been proposed to inhibit SMO by reducing cholesterol abundance in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SM is confined to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.
source: SM is confined to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane and thus its depletion will directly increase accessibility of cholesterol in the outer leaflet (Murate and Kobayashi, 2016; Steck and Lange, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SM depletion will also increase the abundance of cholesterol in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane because cholesterol rapidly redistributes between the two leaflets by flip-flop movement.
source: However, SM depletion (or cholesterol loading) will also increase the abundance of cholesterol in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane because cholesterol rapidly redistributes between the two leaflets of the plasma membrane by flip-flop movement (Steck and Lange, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Exogenously added ALOD4 will trap accessible cholesterol in the outer leaflet but will also consequently reduce cholesterol levels in the inner leaflet.
source: Cholesterol flip-flop between the inner and outer leaflets also means that exogenously added ALOD4 will trap accessible cholesterol in the outer leaflet but will also consequently reduce cholesterol levels in the inner leaflet (Infante and Radhakrishnan, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The predominant sterol in Drosophila is ergosterol, with cholesterol itself representing <5% of membrane sterols.
source: The predominant sterol in Drosophila is ergosterol, with cholesterol itself representing <5% of membrane sterols (Rietveld et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Flies are cholesterol auxotrophs: they acquire cholesterol from their diet and have lost many of the genes for cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: In addition, flies are cholesterol auxotrophs: they acquire cholesterol from their diet and have lost many of the genes for cholesterol biosynthesis (Carvalho et al., 2010; Vinci et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SREBP pathway has been repurposed in Drosophila to respond to phosphatidylethanolamine.
source: The SREBP pathway, which monitors accessible cholesterol in vertebrates, has been repurposed in Drosophila to respond to phosphatidylethanolamine (Dobrosotskaya et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cholesterol levels in Drosophila are sensed by a distinct nuclear receptor-based mechanism.
source: Cholesterol levels in Drosophila are instead sensed by a distinct nuclear receptor-based mechanism (Bujold et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The lack of a need to regulate cholesterol biosynthetic pathway genes abrogates the need to confine HH signaling to primary cilia in insects.
source: We propose that the lack of a need to regulate cholesterol biosynthetic pathway genes abrogates the need to confine HH signaling to primary cilia in insects.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the differences between vertebrates and insects.
